entry.title: Alpine Linux Security Advisory: OpenSSH-server password authentication bypass
entry.content:
Security advisory: openssh-server password authentication bypass

If you run sshd on Alpine Linux, update openssh now and restart sshd. Upgrading the package alone does not replace the running daemon.

If you cannot update yet, at least disable password logins: set PasswordAuthentication no in your sshd configuration and restart sshd. Either one closes the hole.

What is the problem?

An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.

The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is * (an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and needs the machine to have at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash. The attacker then sends a very long password (257 to 1024 bytes). One user with a password is enough: it makes every account without one reachable.

Details are in the OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes. No CVE identifier had been assigned at the time of writing.

Who is affected?

You are affected if all of the following are true:

You run the Alpine openssh-server package, which is built without PAM, or you run openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no. (openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes is not affected.) PasswordAuthentication is yes (the OpenSSH default, unless you changed it). The machine has an account whose password field is *. This includes: root, which ships as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16. OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password protects root, so root is only reachable if PermitRootLogin yes is set. That does not help if another account that can log in is able to become root, for example through doas.Any key-only user created with adduser without a password, or with usermod -p '*'.Users coming from a directory service through musl-nscd (nslcd, winbind, sssd), since they have no shadow entry.The alpine user in the official tiny-cloud images (see below). At least one local account has a $5$ or $6$ password hash.

Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20).

Who is not affected? Docker and other container users that do not run sshd in the container. Systems with PasswordAuthentication no. Systems using openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes (with UsePAM no you are affected). Locked accounts: those with ! as the password field in /etc/shadow (a line starting user:!:). They cannot log in with a password or a key. Systems where no account has a $-style password hash. Cloud images configured through cloud-init, which writes PasswordAuthentication no. How can I fix it? 1. Update apk upgrade -U -a

Alpine 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 contain the fixed package (see the release announcement). The fixed package versions are:

Branch Fixed openssh version edge 10.6_p2-r0 3.24 10.3_p1-r2 3.23 10.2_p1-r1 3.22 10.0_p1-r11 3.21 9.9_p2-r1 3.20 9.7_p1-r6 3.19 9.6_p1-r3 3.18 9.3_p2-r4 3.17 9.1_p1-r7 3.16 9.0_p1-r6

Restart sshd after upgrading (rc-service sshd restart). Upgrading the package does not restart a running sshd, so you must do it after.

2. If you cannot update: disable password authentication

Before you start, make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until you have tested a new login.

Run these as root. The first two commands create a drop-in file. Alpine’s default sshd_config reads that directory from 3.19 onward; older releases ignore it. The sed command changes yes to no on every PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config, whatever the spacing, including lines inside a Match block. It also adds PasswordAuthentication no at the top of the file, for the case where there was no such line, and saves the original as /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak. The last two commands check the configuration, restart the daemon, and show the result:

mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d echo 'PasswordAuthentication no' > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf sed -i.bak -e '1i PasswordAuthentication no' \ -e 's/^\(\s*PasswordAuthentication[^y#]*\)yes/\1no/i' \ /etc/ssh/sshd_config sshd -t && rc-service sshd restart sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication

The last command should print passwordauthentication no. To undo, delete /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf and copy /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak back over /etc/ssh/sshd_config.

Cloud images (tiny-cloud)

The official tiny-cloud images (the qcow2, VHD and AMI artifacts) from 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 ship an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot. They become exploitable as soon as any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example when an admin sets a console password, or user-data adds a user with hashed_passwd. An attacker then gets a shell as alpine and can use doas to become root.

Images built from 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8, 3.24.4 and later include the fixed package. Images from earlier point releases do not, so on every running instance, update openssh or disable password authentication.

Releases that are no longer supported (3.21 and older)

These releases have the same bug. 3.21 reached its end of support on 2026-11-01, but we have published fixed packages for each release all the way back to 3.16.

How do I know if I was attacked?

Look in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password (alpine, root, or any key-only user). Review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys on exposed machines. If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.

How could this happen?

When sshd is built without PAM, it checks a password by hashing the attempt with crypt() (the C library function that turns a password into its stored hash) and comparing the result to the stored password field. For an account whose stored field is too short to contain a salt (the random prefix of a hash), sshd borrows the salt of another account.

musl’s crypt() returns the string * as an error indicator when the key is over 256 bytes long. * is also exactly what the stored field contains for every account with no password, so the “hash” matches and the login succeeds.

OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. The stable-branch packages above carry a patch for the same problem.

Credits

Reported by ÃzgÃ¼n KÃ¼ltekin of Wakefield. Thanks to Damien Miller and Darren Tucker of the OpenSSH project for the fix and the 10.6p2 release, to Timo TerÃ¤s for help analyzing the issue, and to Natanael Copa, who built and uploaded the updated packages.

entry.title: Motorola Signature 27 with GrapheneOS support
The Stacks Project, Formalized in Lean
entry.content:
Today, Axiom is releasing our Lean formalization of the entire Stacks Project, the roughly 7,500-page open-source reference that lays the foundations of modern algebraic geometry. Spanning some 16 million lines of code, it is the largest integrated, reusable library of formalized mathematics ever built.

With this release, the full mathematical development of the Stacks Project is available as a single, machine-checked library. Researchers and AI agents alike can import its definitions and theorems directly into new formal proofs, while permanent Stacks tags link every Lean declaration back to the canonical text mathematicians already know.

This milestone begins with the Stacks Project itself. Initiated by Columbia University mathematician Johan de Jong in 2005, it has grown through the tireless work of hundreds of mathematicians who have contributed proofs, examples, and refinements over two decades. Our formalization rests equally on the foundations of the Lean and Mathlib communities. Formalizing a corpus of this magnitude was only possible because those communities spent years building a rich mathematical library, along with the abstractions needed to organize it, long before our work began.

Why formalize a foundational reference of this scale? As AI systems begin generating mathematical arguments at a pace far beyond what humans can inspect by hand, formal verification becomes essential. In fields with mature Lean infrastructure, new results can often be formalized shortly after they are discovered. Until now, modern algebraic geometry has been far harder to approach this way: a single contemporary proof may invoke a long chain of theorems across commutative algebra, schemes, sheaves, cohomology, and algebraic stacks before its core argument even begins. The mathematics existed in the Stacks Project, but the corresponding Lean infrastructure did not.

Closing that gap is as much a software engineering challenge as a mathematical one. While uncoordinated AI code generation can produce short, isolated scripts quickly, scaling to millions of lines of verified mathematics requires clean abstractions, stable interfaces, and components that fit together across an entire codebase. To achieve this, we deployed coordinated swarms of AI agents capable of translating, proving, and integrating thousands of theorems in parallel. Formalizing the Stacks Project in its entirety establishes a new starting point for algebraic geometry and the many neighboring fields that rely on its machinery.

The mathematics behind Stacks

At its heart, algebraic geometry studies the interplay between algebraic equations and the geometric shapes they describe. Over the real numbers, the equation $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ defines a circle; over the rational numbers, its points correspond to Pythagorean triples, such as $3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2$. Studying the same equations across different number systems, or in families that vary over a parameter space, connects geometry directly to number theory and algebra. These ideas also reach beyond pure mathematics: elliptic curves secure modern digital cryptography, while algebraic curves over finite fields power error-correcting codes. Modern algebraic geometry provides a common language for studying equations across all of these settings.

Forging that language took generations. Emmy Noether revolutionized algebra by shifting focus from individual equations to abstract structures such as rings, modules, and ideals. Just as the right software abstraction can replace thousands of special-purpose routines with a single reusable framework, a theorem proved for the right algebraic structure applies across many concrete settings at once. A generation later, Alexander Grothendieck and his collaborators introduced the theory of schemes, creating a sweeping dictionary between algebra and geometry that allowed mathematicians to do geometry over arbitrary rings, with arithmetic and infinitesimal data built in from the start. Monumental treatises like Éléments de géométrie algébrique (EGA) and Séminaire de géométrie algébrique du Bois Marie (SGA) rebuilt the foundations of the discipline from the ground up, supplying the machinery behind landmark breakthroughs including Deligne’s proof of the Weil conjectures and Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem.

Yet as the subject expanded, its foundational literature grew vast, scattered across thousands of pages of dense monographs and seminars, much of it written in French. A great deal of the subject's working knowledge also lived as unwritten folklore passed down from advisor to student. Even defining an algebraic stack, a geometric space capable of remembering the internal symmetries of the objects it parametrizes, requires a formidable tower of prerequisites spanning commutative algebra, topologies, sheaves, and cohomology. Mathematicians needed a unified, self-contained reference where those prerequisites were written down in full detail.

In 2005, de Jong set out to organize those foundations the way software engineers maintain an open-source project like the Linux kernel. What began as an accessible introduction to algebraic stacks evolved into a living, collaborative encyclopedia comprising thousands of permanent four-character tags. The Stacks Project operates on rigorous editorial principles: every theorem carries a proof, every assumption is stated explicitly, and every step points back to the exact tags on which it depends. In doing so, de Jong and his collaborators anticipated the architecture of formal proof libraries, demonstrating that mathematics becomes far easier to verify and extend when its components have stable identifiers and explicit dependency graphs. Translating the Stacks Project into Lean brings mechanical verification to that human-designed architecture.

A library built for reuse

On October 27, 2026, Axiom released our Lean formalization of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups (CFSG). While CFSG and the Stacks Project are both monumental in scale, they represent fundamentally different engineering challenges. CFSG is organized around a single landmark theorem. The Stacks Project, by contrast, is a foundational library: its value lies in thousands of interlocking definitions, constructions, and lemmas designed to be reused across countless future proofs.

With this library, a mathematician or AI agent formalizing a new theorem about families of curves no longer needs to reconstruct the foundations of schemes or coherent cohomology from scratch. They can import the relevant definitions and theorems directly, while Lean’s kernel guarantees that every cited result is applied only when its exact hypotheses are satisfied. Formalizing the Stacks Project as one connected codebase gives researchers and agents a common chain of verified definitions and theorems on which to build, something no collection of isolated proof scripts can provide.

To make our library easy to navigate, our release preserves the permanent tag structure of the original text. At stacks.axiommath.ai, readers can view the pages of the original Stacks Project side-by-side with the corresponding Lean code and explore the interactive dependency graph. Because a single Stacks tag often unfolds into multiple formal definitions and lemmas, some newly defined and others bridged directly to existing declarations in Mathlib, our interface tracks these mappings explicitly so researchers can see precisely how the informal and formal developments align.

Engineering coherent mathematics at scale

A smorgasbord of independently verified proofs does not make a usable mathematical library. If thousands of AI agents formalize theorems in parallel without architectural coordination, two agents will inevitably prove correct theorems about the same mathematical object using subtly incompatible definitions, or duplicate foundational infrastructure that already exists in Mathlib. Lean’s kernel will accept both files in isolation, but their results will be painfully difficult to compose downstream. Building coherent formal infrastructure requires keeping every definition and interface aligned across the entire project.

At this scale, formalization is as much systems engineering as it is mathematics. To build a single, unified library, our mathematicians and engineers designed a hierarchical system of AI agents with specialized responsibilities and strict coordination protocols. Agents worked in parallel across the dependency graph to translate statements, search Mathlib for existing abstractions, construct proofs, and resolve prerequisites, all while keeping definitions, typeclass interfaces, and mathematical abstractions aligned across chapters.

In a tightly interconnected dependency graph of definitions and theorems, an unfaithful or trivialized formalization is quickly exposed. Ensuring that each formal statement faithfully captures the mathematical meaning of the original text is even more important than verifying its proof. Across the library, statement faithfulness is enforced automatically at scale through multi-agent auditing, semantic cross-checks against the source text, and the strict requirement that every definition and lemma must successfully interface with the downstream theorems that depend on it. Combined with targeted audits on foundational definitions and landmark theorems, this automated verification pipeline ensures that the formal library remains faithful to the mathematics of the Stacks Project.

What formal verification reveals

Over the course of the project, our system surfaced dozens of statements in the Stacks Project that required local refinement, including missing hypotheses, edge cases in positive characteristic, and claims that did not hold in the full generality stated. Rather than treating failed proof attempts as mere obstacles, our agents diagnosed the underlying mathematical obstructions and constructed explicit counterexamples to prove where the original statements broke down.

Once an obstruction was isolated, the system worked to repair the mathematics so downstream chapters could still depend on it. For local oversights, our agents identified the exact missing hypotheses and formalized the corrected theorems alongside their counterexamples. Where a false supporting lemma created a gap in the proof of a deeper theorem, the agents found alternative routes through the literature to establish the main result under its original hypotheses. Together, these resolutions show how large-scale formalization can actively refine and strengthen the mathematical literature itself.

A monument to the past, a foundation for the future

Ultimately, the mathematics inside this library is the product of generations of human creativity, from the geometric intuition of the early pioneers, to the structural revolutions of Noether and Grothendieck, to the open-source scholarship of the Stacks Project and Mathlib communities. Each generation inherited a body of mathematical knowledge, cast it into a sharper language, and handed the next generation a stronger foundation. We see this formalization as part of that ongoing tradition: both a tribute to the mathematicians who built modern algebraic geometry, and working infrastructure for an emerging era in which humans and AI agents explore new mathematical frontiers together.

In an October 21, 2026 announcement, de Jong requested that AI-generated comments and pull requests not be submitted directly to the upstream Stacks Project repository for the time being. The Stacks Project remains an active, living text under the stewardship of Johan de Jong and its community of contributors, while this Lean formalization is an independent open-source project maintained by Axiom. We fully respect that boundary: we keep our formalization, counterexamples, and refinements in our own repository, where mathematicians can review and draw upon them on their own terms.

You can explore the side-by-side text, inspect counterexamples, and trace the full dependency graph at stacks.axiommath.ai. Like the Stacks Project itself, our formalization is open source and designed to grow over time. We invite mathematicians, Lean developers, and AI agents to examine the library, refine its abstractions, and build new mathematics upon it.

entry.title: Window Sweaters
entry.content:
A little Mac app I made to give my windows sweaters. 🧶 Knitted borders, colours inspired by your favourite apps, and a cosier desktop.

window-sweaters-demo-github.mp4

See Window Sweaters in action on X →

You can just send this repo to your coding agent and ask it to install Window Sweaters for you:

Install Window Sweaters on my Mac: https://github.com/saragordic/window-sweaters

Or install it yourself with Homebrew:

brew trust saragordic/tap brew install --cask saragordic/tap/window-sweaters

Then open Window Sweaters from your Applications folder.

You can also grab the latest ZIP from Releases, unzip it, and drag Window Sweaters.app into Applications.

If macOS blocks it, open System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway after trying to launch it. The app isn't notarized by Apple yet. Apple's instructions explain this step.

Click the yarn icon in your menu bar to change the style, pattern, border width, and stitch size. You can also pause the sweaters or quit from there.

To leave an app bare, open Apps and untick it. Its windows lose their sweater straight away, everything else stays as it is, and it stays off until you tick it again, even after a restart. Only want sweaters on a few apps? Choose Turn Off for All Apps, then tick the ones you like. Apps you open later start off too.

By App gives each app its own sweater. Zigzag gives them all a softer, matching cream zigzag in colours taken from their icons. Try both and see what you like.

If macOS asks for Accessibility access, enable Window Sweaters in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility so it can follow which window is focused.

Custom sweaters for 37 apps, and counting! Almost 40 little colourways, with colours picked by hand. These are just a few of my favourites:

Shown above in By App and Zigzag. Here’s everyone we’ve knitted for so far:

Apple: Finder, Safari, Mail, Messages, Notes, Calendar, Reminders, Apple Music, Photos, Preview, Terminal. Work and notes: Notion, Paper, Granola, Microsoft Teams, Slack, Zoom. Coding and AI: Cursor, VS Code, Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Grok Bot, Ghostty. Design: Figma, Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Illustrator. Microsoft Office: Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook. More favourites: Spotify, WhatsApp, Google Chrome, Firefox, Telegram, Discord.

See every sweater and its close-up stitches in the catalogue, or download the By App PDF.

The 37 custom sweaters keep their hand-picked colours and patterns. Other apps borrow colours from their own icons, softened into yarn, and get a two-colour zigzag, picnic or twinkle sweater in By App mode. The pattern stays the same for each app. If an icon has no usable colour, the app keeps a stable colour chosen from its name.

Icons are sampled locally in the background when needed. While the colour is being prepared, the border uses its usual fallback. Zigzag uses icon colours for every app, the 37 custom ones included, with a cream zigzag, or a deeper shade of the app’s colour on pale apps. Colours you set in apps.conf always win. Other shared patterns keep their own contrast yarns, with each app’s own base colour.

I built this on my Mac and use it myself, but there are still rough edges. Borders hide while you resize a window and return when you're done.

The app is built for macOS 13 or later, on Apple Silicon and Intel. I've tested it on Apple Silicon with macOS 26; older macOS versions and Intel Macs haven't had the same hands-on testing. It uses private macOS window APIs, so system updates may affect how it works.

If something looks wrong, open an issue and tell me your macOS version, Mac model, and whether you're using another screen. Reproduction steps help a lot.

You'll need Apple's Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install) and Python 3.

git clone https://github.com/saragordic/window-sweaters.git cd window-sweaters ./scripts/build-app.sh python3 scripts/install-local.py

This builds outputs/Window Sweaters.app, installs it in ~/Applications, and opens it. The installer backs up any previous local installation before replacing it.

If you'd like to experiment, edit these files and restart the app:

~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders/apps.conf ~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders/charts/

The folder still uses the app's original name so existing settings keep working. For example, an app rule looks like this:

Claude = #D58561 atelier-claude

Names match app-name prefixes, ignoring capitalisation; the longest match wins. You can also put your own PNG charts in the charts folder to replace built-in patterns.

If you like setting things up from the command line, Window Sweaters also runs an optional shell script at startup, if you have one at ~/.config/window-sweaters/sweatersrc or ~/.sweatersrc.

Quit Window Sweaters from the yarn icon first. Then, if you installed it with Homebrew:

brew uninstall --zap --cask window-sweaters

--zap also removes your saved colourways. Leave it off to keep them for later.

If you installed it by hand, drag Window Sweaters.app to the Trash, then delete these if you want everything gone:

~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders ~/Library/Preferences/local.knitborders.app.plist

macOS remembers the Accessibility permission separately, so remove Window Sweaters from System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility too.

make test # run the tests make catalogue # render the sweater collection make bench # benchmark the renderer

See CONTRIBUTING.md for more details.

entry.title: Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
entry.content:
4.99 ms p99 cold starts, 72 KB RAM per Actor, scales to billions

Quickstart • Documentation • Blog • Discord • X

Rivet Actors are long-lived processes with in-memory state, a SQLite database, WebSockets, and scheduling. You can create one for each agent, user, session, or tenant.

72 KB per Actor: Actors share a node process instead of each booting a sandbox, so one server holds hundreds of thousands. 4.99 ms p99 cold starts: No image pull and no VM boot. Built for scale: All data lives in S3, so a cluster scales to billions of Actors. Hibernates when idle, wakes on demand: Idle Actors cost nothing and wake on the next request with nothing lost. SQLite backed by S3, at SSD speeds: 1.07 ms durable writes and 1.36 ms reads at p99, for about 10.4× less than replicated SSD storage. Durable & multiplayer AI agents: memory that survives restarts, shared live with every client Workflows: multi-step operations that replay instead of starting over AI-generated apps: run the apps and Actors your agent generates Collaborative editing: one Actor per document, synced to every editor

A minimal agent written from scratch. For a ready-made agent, use Pi Durable.

// server.ts import { actor, setup } from "rivetkit"; import { db } from "rivetkit/db"; import { streamText } from "ai"; import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai"; // One Actor per agent, created on first use: agent.getOrCreate(["agent-123"]) export const agent = actor({ // 1. SQLite: every agent has its own database, so history survives restarts db: db({ onMigrate: async (db) => { await db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (role TEXT, content TEXT)"); }, }), // 2. In-memory state: plain variables that live with the Actor, with no database round trip createVars: () => ({ online: new Map<string, string>() }), // 3. WebSockets: each client holds a live connection, and the Actor pushes to all of them onDisconnect: (c, conn) => { c.vars.online.delete(conn.id); c.broadcast("online", [...c.vars.online.values()]); }, actions: { join: (c, user: string) => { c.vars.online.set(c.conn.id, user); c.broadcast("online", [...c.vars.online.values()]); }, sendMessage: async (c, text: string) => { // Save the message await c.db.execute("INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)", "user", text); const messages = await c.db.execute("SELECT role, content FROM messages"); // Stream tokens to every connected client const response = streamText({ model: openai("gpt-5"), messages }); for await (const delta of response.textStream) { c.broadcast("token", delta); } // Save the response await c.db.execute("INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)", "assistant", await response.text); }, }, }); export const registry = setup({ use: { agent } }); // client.ts (frontend or backend) import { createClient } from "rivetkit/client"; import type { registry } from "./server"; const client = createClient<typeof registry>(); // Open a WebSocket connection to the agent const agent = client.agent.getOrCreate(["agent-123"]).connect(); // Listen for realtime events agent.on("online", users => console.log("online:", users)); agent.on("token", delta => process.stdout.write(delta)); // Call actions on the Actor await agent.join("nathan"); await agent.sendMessage("how many r's in strawberry?");

Each Actor gives the agent a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage for session transcripts and agent artifacts, and hibernation when idle.

Most of an agent's time is spent waiting on inference. When the agent loop runs inside a sandbox, you pay for a whole VM that sits mostly idle with low CPU usage.

Rivet Actors run the agent loop outside of the sandbox instead, often called "separating the head from the hands." The agent's state, memory, and context live in the Actor, and it reaches the sandbox through tools only when it needs to run code. This uses a fraction of the memory and limits the blast radius and trust boundary of the code it runs. Read more about running the harness outside of the sandbox.

Often not. An agent needs a sandbox only to run code it writes. Developers on Rivet use three patterns:

Agents with tools: Many agents only need tool calls, MCP, and APIs, such as customer support or personal agents. No sandbox needed. Agents with a lightweight sandbox: agentOS provides Linux-compatible sandboxing for JS and Python using V8 and WebAssembly, with full POSIX filesystems, networking stacks, and process trees. It covers most workloads, like data analysis, file processing, evals, and code mode. Agents with a full sandbox: Keep your existing sandbox provider and expose its shell and filesystem to the agent as tools, such as a bash tool that runs commands in the sandbox. The Actor reattaches to it across sleeps and restarts. See the sandbox coding agent example.

Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or any coding agent:

Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then ask me what to build and run it locally.

Rivet ships libraries built on top of Actors for common use cases.

Actors: Long-lived processes with state, realtime, and scheduling built in. Agents: Durable agents built on Actors, with memory that survives restarts. Workflows: Multi-step operations built on Actors that replay instead of starting over. agentOS: Run the code your agent writes, securely, with granular control over network access, filesystem access, and resource limits. Dynamic Apps (preview): A backend per user, deployed the moment it is generated. Metric Rivet Actor Sandbox Cold start (p99) 4.99 ms 1.70 s Memory per instance 72.4 KB 512 MiB Storage SQLite on S3 Disk per sandbox Storage cost 10.4× cheaper Replicated SSDs
Benchmark details & methodology Rivet numbers come from the published Rivet Actors vs Cloudflare Durable Objects benchmark, run on Rivet 3.0.3. Its repository has the raw samples and the scripts to reproduce them. Sandbox numbers are for E2B: 512 MiB is its default memory allocation from E2B's billing documentation as of November 4, 2026, and 1.70 s is the p99 cold start from ComputeSDK's October 30, 2026 sandbox benchmark. Storage cost compares S3 Standard with three Amazon EBS gp3 copies at AWS list prices. Sources, dates, and the full method are at rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking. Fault tolerance: If a node goes down, its Actors move elsewhere with their state intact. HTTP & WebSocket networking: Call an Actor over HTTP or hold a live WebSocket to it. End-to-end type safety: Typed clients for your backend and React hooks for your frontend. Cron & scheduling: Wake an Actor on a schedule or at a time it sets for itself. Actor-to-Actor calls: Actors call each other by key across the cluster. Scoped JWTs: Give each client a JWT scoped to the Actors it may reach. OpenTelemetry: Traces, metrics, and logs in OTel format. Option Description Get started Local & self-host Run Rivet locally while you build. In production, run the control plane on Docker, Kubernetes, or a VM. S3 is the only dependency. Self-hosting docs Rivet Cloud Fully managed, dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region. Run your nodes on Rivet Cloud or bring your own. Dashboard BYOC The control plane runs inside your own VPC on AWS, GCP, or Azure, fully managed by Rivet. Your data never leaves your cloud. BYOC docs

Every option runs the same control plane, from local dev to production. Talk to an engineer →

Typed SDKs for your backend and React hooks for your frontend. Rivet runs on native Node.js and Bun with no custom runtime, so your existing packages, tooling, and tests work unchanged.

Deploy nodes on: Docker Compose • Kubernetes • VM & bare metal • Hetzner • AWS ECS • Railway • Render

Runtimes: Node.js • Bun • Rust

Tools: Vitest • OpenTelemetry • Pino • AI SDK • OpenAPI • AsyncAPI

Does Rivet have BYOC?

Yes. Rivet deploys into your own cloud account, including air-gapped environments: the control plane and storage run inside your VPC while Rivet operates them. See the BYOC docs.

Does Rivet have a cloud?

Yes. Rivet Cloud runs fully managed, dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region. It can run your app's Docker image as nodes on Rivet Cloud, or you can bring your own nodes.

Can I self-host Rivet?

Yes. Rivet is fully self-hostable; see the self-hosting docs. The control plane runs anywhere a container runs, with guides for Docker Compose, Kubernetes, VMs and bare metal, Hetzner, Railway, Render, and AWS ECS. For enterprise support with a self-hosted deployment, contact us.

Do I still need Postgres, FoundationDB, or NATS?

No. An object storage bucket is the only dependency: there is no database to run and no message bus, and control plane instances find each other through the bucket. Rivet works with Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, and any S3-compatible store such as MinIO, Cloudflare R2, or Hetzner Object Storage. A local filesystem backend is available for trying Rivet on one machine.

Is Rivet open-source?

Yes. Rivet is open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license. You're looking at it.

Are Rivet Actors only for agents?

No. Rivet is a general actor platform at its core, with nothing specific to agents. For agents, you can use the optional agent library, which runs Pi Durable on Rivet Actors, or write your own agent from scratch.

How does Rivet compare to sandboxes?

A sandbox boots a VM or container per agent, which is slow to start and sits mostly idle. A Rivet Actor runs inside a shared node process: 72 KB and 4.99 ms p99 to start, versus 512 MiB and 1.70 s for a sandbox, and it hibernates when idle. To run untrusted code your agent writes, use agentOS.

How does Rivet compare to Cloudflare Durable Objects?

Rivet is often used as an open-source alternative to Cloudflare Durable Objects that is easy to self-host and scales. It also fixes many of the constraints of Durable Objects: no 128 MB memory cap, bottomless storage instead of a 10 GB SQLite limit, Actors are not randomly evicted, and you control the runtime because Actors run on vanilla Node.js or Bun instead of a custom runtime. Rivet also adds built-in connection handling, event broadcasting, durable scheduling and cron, full Vitest support, lifecycle hooks for draining, and control over Actor upgrades. See the Cloudflare Durable Objects comparison.

Does Rivet use a custom V8 runtime?

No. Rivet runs on native Node.js and Bun, so your existing packages, tooling, and tests work unchanged.

Is Rivet like Erlang, Akka, or Orleans?

Rivet implements the virtual actor pattern, which is closest to Orleans, but focuses on what modern workloads need: SQLite persistence instead of simple JSON stores and support for modern runtimes. Erlang and Akka do not provide virtual actors out of the box, though ecosystem packages exist that offer functionality comparable to Rivet Actors.

Does Rivet require microVMs, gVisor, or nested virtualization?

No. Rivet only needs a standard process that connects to the control plane over WebSocket. That process can be Node.js, Bun, Rust, or anything else.

entry.title: The Hackintosh Reborn
entry.content:
The Hackintosh Reborn... with AI

Almost a decade ago, I released a hackintosh guide on running macOS 10.14 through a VM with an x86 host. A "Hackintosh" is the feat of running macOS on non-Apple hardware, and has a history dating back to the late 1980s. At the time KVM and PCI passthrough were relatively new technologies, and this guide provided near-native performance with GPU acceleration.

A few years passed by, and we saw Apple release the first ARM-based Mac in 2021, the M1 MacBook Air. The timing was impeccable, Intel was unable to create competitive processors (due to being stuck on the 14nm node), and Apple had powerful and efficient ARM chips already being shipped in their iPhones. The long battery life, the fanless design, the instant wake, what's not to like? The benefits of switching to ARM were clear, however to most, this was thought to be the final chapter in the hackintosh community. x86 versions of macOS would soon be discontinued, and the hackintosh community would slowly fade away. That day has come and the latest version of macOS 27 (Golden Gate) released this year is no longer compatible with x86...

Just a few days ago, I decided to create an iOS app for the first time. It required XCode 26 for development, so I used my spare ThinkPad T490 as my development machine and installed macOS 26 using a posted guide. The installation was smooth and painless. XCode 26 has integrations with Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, and this was my first foray into AI-assisted coding. After some initial tinkering with x86 workarounds, I was pleased that I had a functional iOS app within a day, without touching a single line of code!

So how does this all tie in? Well, this is exactly what the Hackintosh community could hardly envision five years ago: the rise of AI. Waiting patiently and gently until now, the hackintosh and the hackios community has seen an absolute explosion in development, activity, and success in the past few weeks! As one person aptly wrote, this is the power of Claude Code with Ghidra on steroids. Just to list a few recent developments, we have:

macOS 27 running on the Snapdragon Laptop:

macOS 27.2 Beta on an ARM SBC RK3588 with Mali drivers:

iOS 17 running on the Nintendo Switch OLED:

Support for 50-series Nvidia GPUs with nullmoth:

I'm barely scratching the surface, with further developments in AirDrop, accelerated video decode, and even running translated macOS 27 on x86. As much as we lament the cost of AI, there are some glimmers of hope: you just might be able to have your hardware and own it too.

entry.title: Introducing Pangram Image 1.0
entry.content:
Introducing Pangram Image 1.0

State-of-the-art AI image and video detection with our latest Pangram Image models.

Introducing Pangram Image 1.0 and Pangram Image Flash 1.0

A real photograph containing an AI image. Pangram Image 1.0 is able to locate the AI content with its heatmap.

A few months ago, we released Pangram Image as a research preview. We are now proud to announce Pangram Image 1.0: The state-of-the-art in both AI image and AI video detection. We would like to thank the whole community for taking the time to try it and find its weaknesses, and for holding us to a high standard to make a better detector for everyone.

What’s new Our new flagship AI image detection model, Pangram Image 1.0, with: State-of-the-art performance at detecting frontier AI image generatorsHeatmap output for localizing exactly where AI appears in imagesRobustness to edits, compression, and low resolutions A smaller, faster model, Pangram Image Flash 1.0, with: State-of-the-art performance at detecting frontier AI video generatorsFrame by frame analysis of AI edited videos Chrome Extension support for detecting AI in your feed API support for image and video Try it here Pangram Image 1.0 Frontier Image Detection

We tested our Pangram Image 1.0 model against several commercial and academic AI image detectors. We created synthetic mirrors of 100 real photos using 12 frontier state of the art AI image generators, using prompts that closely matched the original photo for a total of 1,200 synthetic images. Our model achieves 99.96% accuracy on this evaluation set.

Academic AI Image Detection Benchmarks

We are committed to providing the highest quality detection to our users. To test our model robustly, we compared it against several academic benchmarks for AI image detection.

Sources: X-AIGD · Mirage-Test · AIGenImages2026 · Synthbuster + RAISE comparison · Community Forensics

Robustness

Many social media platforms compress and downscale images, and malicious actors can also add blur, noise, and other artifacts to try to trick AI detectors into thinking AI images are real. We specifically train to detect these kinds of transformations, and we have found our model to be robust to these edits.

Low Resolution Detection

Our initial release limited image input to the minimum size of 512x512, as our accuracy dropped off at lower resolutions. We are now lowering this limit to 256x256, as we find our new model has improved accuracy at lower resolutions. At resolutions below 512, image detection results will come with a reduced confidence disclaimer.

Video Detection Pangram Image Flash 1.0

A recent academic study, DF26, showed that humans are barely better than random when it comes to telling real videos from AI videos of people talking. Modern detectors were not much better. This is why we are very excited to release Pangram Image Flash 1.0, a faster model that particularly excels at frontier AI video detection. On DF26 it scores 98.7%, a 29-point leap over the next best detector.

Industry Comparison

To compare against the industry, we took 129 real social media videos and generated AI mirrors using 14 different frontier video generators (100 videos each, sampled from the 129 real videos). The generators were each seeded with the first real frame from the input video and then prompted with a VLM-generated description of what happens in the video to make a difficult synthetic mirror. We then compared our model against multiple major AI video detection services across the 1,529 total videos:

An example of a real video (left) and its synthetic mirror (right). Could you tell which is real?

By starting from real video frames and creating a synthetic mirror, we can evaluate the model’s ability to distinguish between two very realistic looking videos. This prevents the model from introducing bias towards calling certain types of content AI, since each real video and its mirror share the same scene and subject.

Academic AI Video Detection Benchmarks

We compare our Image Flash model against several academic benchmarks for frontier AI video detection. We achieve state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks, which together include almost every frontier generation model for AI video.

Sources: AIGVDBench · DF26 · Ivy-Fake

Native Video Support

Pangram now natively supports video upload. Upload a video and Pangram Image Flash 1.0 will analyze it frame by frame to give you a complete analysis of which parts of the video come back as AI detected.

Chrome Extension

We have integrated Pangram Image 1.0 into our Chrome extension. This will flag AI-generated content while you scroll social media, online shopping, rental listings, and any other site where knowing that what you’re seeing is real matters.

API

With the release of Pangram Image 1.0 and Flash 1.0, we updated our API to support both image and video detection. We are excited to put the capability of these models into the hands of the community.

Isaac is a research engineer working on AI image/video detection at Pangram. He recently worked on 2D and 3D detection at Samsung AI Center NYC and has his Master’s in Robotics from the University of Minnesota.

entry.title: Goodbye from Salon
entry.content:
Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

Itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

We also want to thank our readers. You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered. You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us.

The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

Salon

entry.title: Tencent Launches Hy4, One of the Leading Open-Source AI Models
entry.content:
Tencent today announced the release of Tencent Hy4, its latest-generation large language model, marking a significant leap in performance and capabilities that now ranks it among the world’s leading open-source AI models. Tencent Hy plans to release model weights and system cards in the coming days, reinforcing its commitment to responsible open-source AI development, with a focus on cybersecurity and biological safety.

The new model also introduces visual understanding capabilities for the first time, alongside major improvements in instruction following, long-context comprehension and long-horizon agentic tasks, delivering stronger overall performance across a diverse set of applications.

Through advanced visual understanding, reasoning, and tool-calling capabilities, Hy4 now supports a broader range of tasks, including fine-grained image processing, complex chart analysis, and mathematical visual reasoning.

Additionally, Hy4 introduces computer-use capabilities for the first time, enabling it to interact with both command-line interfaces and graphical user interfaces to perform a wide range of work and everyday tasks. The model has undergone specialized training on professional software such as Blender and CAD, significantly enhancing its ability to plan and execute long-horizon and sophisticated tasks.

Deep Model-Product Co-Design Unlocks New Opportunities for Real-World Productivity

Leveraging significant advances in its foundational capabilities and deep model-product co-design, Hy4 unlocks a broader range of real-world productivity scenarios:

Office Productivity & Collaboration: Hy4 has significantly enhanced the user experience on Tencent WorkBuddy. Evaluation benchmarks on WorkBuddy show an average performance score of 83.18 and a pass rate of 96.15 percent, with Hy4 ranking first place in nine out of twelve scenarios within the mainland Chinese market. In practical use, Hy4 balances efficiency and effectiveness for visual creative tasks, 3D scene construction, and web development. Furthermore, it delivers marked improvements in document presentation, stability, and usability for human-AI collaborative tasks on WorkBuddy.

Leveraging enhanced in-context learning capabilities, Hy4 excels at understanding complex information from diverse sources. Integrated with WeCom via WorkBuddy, Hy4 connects with daily workflow data across chats, emails, documents, calendars, and meetings. When managing multiple projects simultaneously, Hy4 automatically tracks project history and recent developments. It identifies outstanding tasks, flags upcoming meetings that require preparation, and monitors approaching deadlines, helping users prioritize effectively and stay aligned on important follow-ups. In addition, new team collaboration capabilities powered by Hy4 will be introduced with the upcoming release of WorkBuddy’s “Projects” feature.

Hy4 has also been optimized for professional financial analysis. By training on thousands of specialized workspaces and tens of thousands of high-quality tasks derived from real-world scenarios, the model gains a deep understanding of expert workflows in fund research, securities analysis, and quantitative investment strategies.

In a rigorous blind evaluation conducted by the Tencent Hy team in partnership with Tencent Financial Technology, Hy4 emerged as the top-performing open-source model. The assessment involved 213 financial professionals, including 153 experts from leading external institutions, approximately 70 percent of whom possessed more than five years of industry experience. Based on performance across 579 real-world financial tasks, Hy4 achieved the highest overall performance score.

Evaluation scores: Hy4 (3.04), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (2.97), Kimi K3.1 Pro (2.68), and GLM-5.3 (2.68).

In addition, Hy4 achieved a 12.03 percentage-point improvement over Hy4 Preview in the internal Investment Research Agent Benchmark (iRaB) evaluation conducted by financial AI company Rabyte.

To enhance the model’s real-world applicability across financial and other workplace scenarios, Tencent Hy has also introduced targeted search optimisation that focuses on retrieving up-to-date information, integrating multiple information sources, and verifying factual consistency. In internal evaluations, Hy4 reduced its hallucination rate from 12.95% in the Hy4 Preview to 7.2%, while errors caused by unsupported assumptions fell from 23.1% to 5.6%.

Frontend & Game Development: Hy4 is optimized for high-complexity tasks, including intricate business logic, state management, front-end and back-end orchestration. This ensures that generated interfaces are not only visually polished but also fully functional. Furthermore, through collaboration with Tencent Interactive Entertainment Group (IEG) professional developers, Hy4 has significantly advanced its game development capabilities. By deeply integrating with major engines like Unreal Engine (UE), Unity, and Godot, the model now supports complex game logic and multiplayer implementations. Compared to Hy4 Preview, Hy4 improved by 19.1 percent in GameDev and 9.8 percent in GameLogic benchmarks.

Scientific Research: Hy4 combines advanced reasoning, scientific programming, and long-horizon task execution to support complex, end-to-end research workflows. Validated with TenureTrail, which assessed 123 executable tasks across seven disciplines, the model demonstrated superior performance in mathematical construction, physical modeling, environmental and earth sciences, systems engineering, and socio-economic decision-making.

Hy4 is advancing into the next stage of Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) to further enhance its model research and development capabilities. Leveraging the Hyra 2.0 harness, Hy4 optimized the pre-training infrastructure for smaller models sharing the same architecture. Additionally, the Hy team has open-sourced two foundational models developed with Hy4 and Hyra 2.0 for single-cell representations (HyCell) and the physics fields (HyPDE). These tools are designed to provide the research community with robust, reusable assets for scientific discovery.

Advancing Responsible Open-Source AI through Cybersecurity and Biosafety Safeguards

Tencent Hy is committed to advancing responsible open-source AI, incorporating safeguards throughout model training and release, with a strong emphasis on cybersecurity and biosafety to support the safe and responsible use of AI.

Cybersecurity: Hy4 is trained on defensive security data, prioritizing proof-of-concept (PoC) development and vulnerability remediation. The model incorporates reverse engineering and penetration testing for analysis purposes. However, offensive materials related to exploitation are explicitly excluded from the training dataset.

Cybersecurity experts from Tencent’s Xuanwu Lab and Keen Security Lab conducted security assessments covering cryptographic reverse engineering, binary deobfuscation, vulnerability exploitation, and more. The assessments found no significant concerns regarding Hy4’s offensive cybersecurity capabilities in the areas evaluated.

Biosafety: Based on internal expert reviews, Hy4 demonstrates strong foundational biological knowledge; however, its capabilities in open-ended experimental design are more limited compared to frontier models.

Delivering Greater Cost Performance, Hy4 Flash Recently Released

Hy4 is currently available across Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy, CodeBuddy, Yuanbao, WeCom’s AI Assistant (Dayuan), ima, and more. Additionally, the model’s API is being made available via third-party platforms such as OpenRouter, Hermes, and OpenCode. Integration efforts are underway for other Tencent products and platforms, including QQ, Honor of Kings, Game of Peace, WeRead, and Tencent News.

Guided by a core commitment to practical AI, Hy4 continues to push the boundaries of AI performance while delivering exceptional cost-effectiveness. Despite significant performance improvements over Hy4 Preview, Hy4 maintains the same pricing: approximately US$0.90 per million input tokens, US$2.70 per million output tokens and US$0.045 per million cached input tokens.

Hy4 Flash is scheduled for release soon and will deliver greater cost-efficiency for users who prioritize high-value applications.

From November 4 to 15, WorkBuddy and CodeBuddy will be available for free. In addition, Hy4 will be available on Tencent Cloud TokenHub at 50% off its standard pricing, with this offer running through December 31, 2026.

entry.title: Cuban: Facebook knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads; docs say $16B fraud revenue
entry.content:
Mark Cuban keeps getting emails about a $294 diabetes cure he has never sold.

"Every single week I get emails from little old men and ladies saying, 'Will my cure for diabetes work?' or 'I just ordered your cure for diabetes for $294,'" the 68-year-old billionaire investor said on an August episode of Pivot, the podcast hosted by Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway.

Those ads are deepfakes built with an AI copy of his face and voice, Cuban said, and Meta (NASDAQ:META) runs them anyway. "Facebook knows the little old ladies are getting ripped off," he said. He called the platform "the worst of the worst."

The ads Cuban says Meta waves through

Cuban said some of the ads even include a disclaimer admitting the person on screen is AI-generated and the clip is meant as entertainment. By the time anyone gets to it, he argued, the pitch has already worked. "And to Facebook, that's good enough," he said.

"The point is, that defines the culture of the organization," Cuban said. A company that lets scammers go after people's grandparents, he argued, has shown what it will tolerate at every level.

Cuban does run a drug company — he co-founded Cost Plus Drugs, an online pharmacy that sells low-cost generic medications.

What Meta's documents showed

On Nov. 6, 2025, Reuters reported on internal Meta documents showing the company expected roughly $16 billion, or about 10% of its 2024 revenue, to flow in from ads pushing scams and prohibited products. By Meta's own internal count, users across its apps were seeing some 15 billion "higher risk" ads a day — the ones with obvious markers of fraud. One late 2024 document put that category's value at about $7 billion a year.

In a May 2025 presentation, Meta's own safety staff estimated the company's platforms play a part in a third of the scams that succeed in the U.S. Before Meta bans an advertiser, its automated systems must peg the account as at least 95% likely to be running a scam, the documents say. Below that threshold, the suspected scammer simply pays more per ad and stays live.

Meta spokesman Andy Stone told Reuters the documents "present a selective view that distorts Meta's approach to fraud and scams," and called the company's 10% estimate "rough and overly-inclusive." Complaints from users about scam ads had fallen 58% over the prior 18 months, he said at the time, and the company pulled down more than 134 million scam ads in 2025. The same documents note the Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into Meta over advertising tied to financial fraud.

entry.title: Brazilian Credit Guarantor Fund Data Breach Affecting PII and Payout Data
entry.content:
Comunicado importante

Atualização em 05/11/2026.

O FGC informa sobre um incidente de segurança envolvendo dados pessoais tratados pela entidade e esclarece o que foi identificado, as providências adotadas e os cuidados que recomendamos.

Identificamos acesso não autorizado a informações pessoais em ambientes relacionados aos processos internos do fluxo de pagamento de garantia do FGC. Até o momento, não foi identificada nenhuma evidência de que os dados tenham sido divulgados ou utilizados de forma indevida. Também não foi identificada nenhuma perda financeira decorrente do evento. A investigação prossegue, com apoio de empresas especializadas, para esclarecer a extensão do acesso e verificar se houve cópia, divulgação ou utilização indevida das informações.

A suspeita de incidente foi identificada em 26 de outubro de 2026. Desde então, foram adotadas restrições de acesso aos ambientes envolvidos, bloqueio de contas indevidas, preservação de evidências e revisão das permissões e dos controles de segurança.

A Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) foi devidamente comunicada, em conformidade com a legislação vigente. A apuração continua, com apoio de especialistas, e as informações complementares pertinentes serão encaminhadas à Agência conforme o avanço das investigações. Os titulares afetados também foram comunicados.

Reunimos aqui as informações disponíveis e confirmadas nesta etapa. Caso a apuração identifique novos elementos relevantes relacionados a dados pessoais ou as medidas de proteção, atualizaremos as orientações pelos canais oficiais.

Quais dados foram afetados:

Dados pessoais: nome, CPF, e-mail e data de nascimento; Dados relacionados ao pagamento da garantia: informações sobre os tributos retidos no pagamento e sobre o canal de distribuição pelo qual o investimento garantido foi realizado na instituição liquidada.

Principais cuidados e como se proteger

As informações envolvidas podem ser utilizadas para tornar contatos fraudulentos mais convincentes, inclusive em tentativas de uso indevido de identidade ou de obtenção de pagamentos e outras informações pessoais.

Por essa razão, enviamos comunicação aos titulares afetados e recomendamos atenção redobrada a mensagens, ligações e e-mails que mencionem informações pessoais ou relacionadas ao pagamento da garantia, especialmente quando realizadas por pessoas que se apresentem como representantes do FGC ou de outras instituições. Qualquer pessoa, ao receber algum contato suspeito, pode entrar em contato com o FGC.

Destacamos alguns cuidados importantes para a segurança de todos:

Desconfie de contatos que solicitem pagamentos, senhas, códigos de autenticação ou instalação de aplicativos, mesmo quando mencionarem informações corretas sobre você;

Não clique em links em mensagens suspeitas. Para acessar informações do processo de pagamento, use diretamente o aplicativo do FGC;

Confirme informações relacionadas ao processo de pagamento de garantia pelos canais oficiais do FGC;

Preserve as mensagens suspeitas e registre ocorrência perante as autoridades competentes se identificar tentativa de fraude. Neste caso, avise imediatamente o FGC.

Como os dados são protegidos e o que estamos fazendo

A segurança da informação é prioridade para o FGC que possui arquitetura robusta de proteção, além de equipes especializadas que atuam no monitoramento, na detecção e resposta a ameaças. Os ambientes utilizavam mecanismos de autenticação e controle de acesso. Após a identificação do incidente, restringimos os acessos aos ambientes envolvidos, desabilitamos contas indevidas, reforçamos o monitoramento e preservamos evidências para a investigação. A revisão de permissões e a validação dos controles de segurança permanecem em andamento.

O tema está sendo tratado com a máxima prioridade, tendo como principal preocupação o apoio aos titulares de dados afetados e a revisão contínua dos mecanismos de proteção de dados e de segurança da informação.

Atualizações e orientações sobre o incidente serão disponibilizadas nesta página: fgc.org.br/comunicado.

Para obter mais detalhes sobre dados pessoais ou esclarecer dúvidas específicas, entre em contato com nossa central de atendimento pelo e-mail: atendimento.credores@fgc.org.br.

Seguimos à disposição para prestar esclarecimentos e apoiar você nas medidas de prevenção.

Atenciosamente,

Fundo Garantidor de Créditos - FGC Encarregado de dados – DPO privacidade@fgc.org.br

Today we are introducing our second model generation with Inkling 2 Small. It is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 594B total parameters, 17B active, and supports image inputs and variable effort.

Inkling 2 Small far surpasses our previous models’ scores on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 31, reflecting gains in performance on agentic coding, vision, knowledge work, and reasoning. The increase in capabilities comes from improvements made at every step of our training process, including more efficient pre-training and a large, unified RL run.

Inkling 2 Small will initially be available through Tinker, with closed weights, following the approach we outlined in a safe path to open weights. We intend to make the full weights available under an Apache 2.0 license next week after the completion of external safety testing and red-teaming.

You can try Inkling 2 Small on Tinker Playground today. The model is also available for fine-tuning and sampling on Tinker; checkpoints will be downloadable with the release of Inkling 2 Small’s weights.

Capabilities

Inkling 2 Small is more capable across the board than our first generation, particularly in long-horizon autonomous work.

Inkling 2 Small’s vision and agentic capabilities enable it to incorporate visual feedback to iteratively build and refine websites, games, and 3D designs with interactive elements.

Agentic coding and autoresearch

Inkling 2 Small was trained with RL on hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding tasks across multiple agent harnesses and context-compaction strategies. We increased the quality of our synthetic coding data pipeline and moved beyond unit-test rewards alone; many tasks included an agentic RL grader that evaluated how the model approached the problem, not just whether its code passed. We also tested early checkpoints of Inkling 2 Small on OpenCode under the name Fledge-Alpha to assess our model’s performance on coding tasks in the real world.

The result is a model that is both stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops. Inkling 2 Small improves on usability compared to Inkling: it follows instructions better, considers changes carefully, and verifies its work without being asked.

When tasks were difficult, early checkpoints of Inkling 2 Small were persistent in trying to succeed—in some cases fabricating results, ignoring instructions, and concealing what they had done.

We worked across the stack to improve model alignment. In midtraining, we filtered out traces containing misbehavior and included traces with honest, aligned behavior. In RL, we added a general alignment reward that penalizes misbehavior on every task. We also built environments targeting specific failure modes we observed in training, such as rewarding models for giving up on impossible tasks. Finally, we used on-policy self-distillationZhao et al., 2026. from a teacher model prompted with a conduct spec, so the model internalizes principles for good behavior without explicit prompting.

We measured progress with both internal and external evaluations, and found that Inkling 2 Small substantially improves over previous Inkling models on both internal and external evaluations, and outperforms a set of comparable open-weights models on our internal evals.

Inkling 2 Small still trails closed-weights models, such as GPT-6.1 Sol on our alignment evaluations. Reducing this gap is a priority for future models.

We also worked to secure training and evaluations with two layers of monitoring. The first is synchronous: a monitor inspects tool calls before they run. Each task declares what actions it authorizes. Deterministic rules check calls against the task’s policy and circumvention patterns, escalating uncertain cases to an LLM judge. The second layer is asynchronous: an LLM judge reviews completed rollouts from training and evaluation for misbehavior and actions against our security boundary, raising alerts that we triage and escalate into our incident process. Together, these form a defense-in-depth approach to safety and alignment that we consider critical to developing a safe model factory.

Training Inkling 2 Small

Inkling 2 Small’s initial pretraining phase (H1) covered 8.4 trillion tokens of a broad mix of natural language, code, and image data. It ran for 68 hours on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks, which enabled high expert parallelism. Training ran natively in NVFP4, the 4-bit floating-point format introduced with the NVIDIA Blackwell GPU architecture. We’ll share more details on our NVFP4 recipe in a follow-up post soon.

We followed this initial phase with a second phase (H2) of 3.8 trillion tokens of higher-quality, newer data the model hadn’t seen, at 512K context. The third and fourth phases mixed in data in the deployment format. The third phase was about 320 billion tokens of reasoning and agent trajectories at 1M context, alongside replayed pretraining data. The fourth phase (H4) kept only the highest-quality data: about 34 billion tokens of agent trajectories. The H3 and H4 mixtures consisted mostly of trajectories sampled from earlier models including Kimi K3 and our own models, filtered for correctness and alignment.

We then carried out a joint RL run, consisting of 1,075 steps and over 17 million rollouts over 9 days. See table below for more details. This single joint run contrasts with the previous Inkling release, where we ran separate reasoning and agentic RL runs and combined them with multi-teacher distillation.

Scale of the main RL run Metric Scale Compute Over 4 × 10²³ FLOPs GPUs 2,048 Duration 9 days Rollouts 17M+ Tokens 3T+

The task mix included software engineering in real repositories, terminal tasks, document creation, STEM question answering, vision, web app building, tool use with simulated users, and safety. Each task family had its own grader:

hidden unit tests and programmatic checks for most coding work;

rubric-based LLM judges for documents and tool use;

reference answers for STEM and vision question answering;

pairwise reward models comparing screenshots of rendered web apps.

We randomly sampled and conditioned on an effort level, and applied a length penalty in the reward function, which trained the model to trade off speed and thoroughness.

Our asynchronous RL uses a score centering variant—the StableReinforce objective in Tinker—which tolerates significant staleness. Our run combines short and long horizon tasks with p50/p99 total rollout tokens being 43k and 1.5M respectively and p50/p99 duration of 8 minutes and 4 hours respectively. We use 256k context length and enable compaction training for long-horizon tasks. As a result, both training reward and evaluation performance grow log-linearly with compute.

Stable training Metric Value Median policy staleness 17 updates Rollout batch size 16K Total tokens per rollout Median: 43K · p99: 1.5M Rollout duration Median: 8 minutes · p99: 4 hours Context window 256K tokens, with compaction for longer trajectories

Making this scale practical required improvements throughout the systems stack. Our RL infrastructure deploys NVFP4 MoE training and sampling. During sampling, prefill, draft, and verify run fully on CUDA graphs. Trainers mirror the pretrain stack with high expert parallelism, EPLB, and CUDA graphs to improve GPU efficiency. To support long horizon agentic workloads, we use sticky routing and DRAM KV-cache offloading for maintaining 93%+ prefix cache hit rate, allowing us to maintain a 5:3 sampler:trainer ratio despite training at long contexts. Weight transfer is done via GPUDirectRDMA at 93%+ line rate with a parallelism-invariant checksum verifier. We also further lower deployment inference cost by offering a variant of NVFP4 KV cache, which we find to minimally lower evals.

Long-horizon tasks give the model hours of autonomy, increasing potential risks from misaligned behavior. Midway through the main RL run, our asynchronous monitor flagged an instance where the model, failing at a task, worked around a network block through a third-party service it could reach using its search tools. We paused the run, hardened our infrastructure, removed environments that required web access, and added synchronous tool-call monitoring. We then resumed the run, incorporating additional training phases specifically for alignment, as described above.

Improvements to our process allow us to train models at different sizes using similar recipes with predictable scaling and performance. Inkling 2 Small is part of a ladder of models; we look forward to sharing more rungs with you soon.

While Inkling 2 Small improves on usability vs Inkling, it is not the most succinct communicator, and doesn’t always choose the best tools for the job—especially in codebases with a large number of skills.

Like previous Inkling models, Inkling 2 Small natively supports image input; however, this model does not support audio.

Inkling 2 Small is also less optimized for the chat experience. We notice issues such as worse organization and presentation of content, overuses of slashes, and overreaction to mental health and other safety related queries.

Inkling 2 Small was made in service of our mission to build AI that extends human will and judgment. We hope that it encourages your ambitions, and we look forward to seeing what you build with it.

MoofTCP – A modern replacement for MacTCP on 68k Macs
entry.content:
A modern, memory-lean replacement for MacTCP on 68k Macs running System 6.

MoofTCP is a drop-in replacement for Apple's MacTCP. Programs written for MacTCP run on it unchanged, but underneath it is a fresh TCP/IP stack written from scratch in portable C, with its own control panel, installer and DHCP client. It was built for a Mac Classic with 4 MB of RAM, so every byte counts.

MacTCP is wonderful, but it is old, and on a 4 MB Mac Classic with a SCSI Wi-Fi/Ethernet adapter like BlueSCSI it can be slow to answer, hungry for memory, and awkward to set up. MoofTCP aims, in this order, for:

Reliability. No hangs, no leaks, no surprises when apps quit. Low latency for interactive use, like typing in a telnet session. Throughput, for handling quasi-modern use cases.

...all while using no more resident memory than MacTCP does.

Drop-in compatible. Implements the MacTCP .IPP driver interface (TCP, UDP, ICMP echo) and the dnrp name resolver. Your existing MacTCP programs just work. DHCP or a fixed address. Pick either in the control panel. Don't need to manage static IP anymore. MoofTCP Lite. A build without DHCP that saves about 5 KB of system memory, for tight machines. One installer holds both; a checkbox picks which one. A friendly installer. It moves MacTCP's files aside, installs MoofTCP, and its Remove button puts everything back exactly as it was. An interrupted install repairs itself. MultiFinder-aware. Quitting an app that had connections open cleans up after it. Built-in diagnostics. An optional in-memory log and a small MoofDiag tool for bug reports. A portable core. The TCP/IP stack in core/ has no malloc and no global state, and is tested on the desktop with sanitizers and fuzzers. Installer MoofTCP Lite panel
Download MoofTCP-1.0.dsk, MoofTCP-1.0.hqx or MoofTCP-1.0.sit from the Releases page and get it onto your Mac (a BlueSCSI shared folder works well). Open MoofTCP Installer, leave Lite version (no DHCP) unticked, and click Install. Restart the Mac. Open Control Panels, MoofTCP, enter your IP address, mask, router and DNS server (or tick Get the address by DHCP), and save. Restart again. You're online.

To go back to MacTCP, run the installer and click Remove. The Read Me file in the release has the details, including how to switch between MoofTCP and MoofTCP Lite.

StuffIt Lite 3.6 is tested as working for expanding the .hqx packages.

A 68k Mac with System 6.0.8 (the version it was tested on). Please report back if it works on other versions! An Ethernet adapter that provides the .ENET0 driver, such as a BlueSCSI v2 WiFi with DaynaPORT. MoofTCP does not include an Ethernet driver.

Tested on a real Mac Classic (System 6.0.8, 4 MB, BlueSCSI v2 WiFi with DaynaPORT) and in the Snow emulator.

Program Result Flynn (telnet terminal) Works, real Mac and emulator Wikipedia Reader Works, real Mac and emulator MacTCP Watcher Works in the emulator NCSA Telnet Works in the emulator Fetch (FTP) Works in the emulator TurboGopher Works in the emulator Eudora Starts; mail was not tried

Have a program that doesn't work? Please open an issue (see below).

MoofTCP MoofTCP Lite Driver code 95,623 bytes 90,722 bytes Free system heap after first open (real Mac Classic, single Finder, full build) about 30.7 KB n/a

MultiFinder grows the system heap on demand, so free memory varies more there.

MoofTCP keeps a small diagnostic log in memory. If a program misbehaves but the Mac keeps running, run MoofDiag right away (it is in the release's diagnostic tools download), and open an issue with the MoofDiag.out file it writes next to itself, plus a note about what you were doing. Feel free to ask your LLM to analyze the codebase and the diagnostic output as well and to submit fix PRs.

No IPv6. Tested only with the DaynaPORT Ethernet driver on System 6.0.8. DHCP is basic: no lease RELEASE, no INIT-REBOOT and no address-conflict probe. While it runs, programs cannot use UDP port 68. With no DHCP server, the first open waits about 10 seconds and then fails.

You only need Docker. The pinned Retro68 cross-compiler image is pulled automatically.

scripts/build-mac.sh MoofTCP # the MoofTCP file -> build-mac/moof/ MT_LITE=1 scripts/build-mac.sh MoofTCP # MoofTCP Lite -> build-mac-lite/ scripts/release.sh --force 1.0 # one installer with both -> dist/MoofTCP-1.0.{dsk,hqx,sit}

release.sh also needs hfsutils, macutils, unar, gcc and Python 3.

The portable core and the glue logic are tested on your desktop with gcc and CMake (AddressSanitizer and UBSan are on by default):

cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure cmake -S . -B build-lite -DMT_NO_DHCP=ON # the Lite configuration

The emulator tests (Snow) need Apple system software and the BlueSCSI DaynaPORT image. Those are not in this repository and you must supply them yourself; the scripts in scripts/ (setup-home.sh, golden-stage.sh) show what is expected.

core/ portable TCP/IP stack (no malloc, no globals), host-tested mac/ Mac glue: .IPP driver, INIT, resolver, control panel, installer, diagnostic apps tests/ host tests (ctest), including fuzzers scripts/ build, release, emulator and hardware-session scripts tools/ pinned tool versions; tools/sit is a small StuffIt-format writer

Bug reports, compatibility reports ("program X does/doesn't work") and pull requests are welcome. For code changes, please read CONTRIBUTING.md and run the host tests first (see above). CLAUDE.md is a detailed map of the code and its rules. Security problems: see SECURITY.md.

Retro68 for the 68k cross-compiler. Snow for the Mac emulator the tests run in. BlueSCSI and DaynaPORT for the network hardware this was built around. Claude Code was used to develop this project, with human planning and testing. More comprehensive bake-in testing on real hardware as we use it Remake Daynaport similarly (stay tuned for MoofPort) Review the BlueSCSI codebase for opportunities to integrate more tightly for better performance There is potential for further algorithm optimization for added performance on smaller or older systems.

MIT. "MacTCP" and "StuffIt" are trademarks of their owners and are used here only to describe compatibility. MoofTCP contains no Apple or third-party code; building it uses Apple's interfaces as shipped in the Retro68 toolchain.
